intro: A sample is only as good as the way it was chosen. Pick a method, draw a sample from an illustrated population, and watch where the sample mean lands. Draw a hundred samples and the dots show the two things that matter: whether a method is biased (centered away from the truth) and how much it varies.
howItWorksTitle: How the lab draws its samples
howItWorks:
Each population is fixed: every household, plot or student has its own value, made once from a seed, so the population mean never changes. Every sample comes from a seeded random number generator.

  • Simple random. Random integers from 1 to N, repeats skipped, until n different labels appear.
  • Stratified. The sample is split among the strata in proportion to their sizes, then a simple random sample is taken inside each stratum.
  • Cluster. Whole groups (streets, rows, classrooms) are chosen at random; everyone in them is in the sample.
  • Systematic. k = N ÷ n, rounded down; a random start from 1 to k, then every k-th label.
  • Convenience. The units nearest the spot where the surveyor stands.
  • Voluntary response. Everyone is invited, and the chance of answering grows with how strongly a unit feels, so the strongest opinions answer most.

Test yourself makes new problems from a seed (the problem code) and checks every step against a key the validator recomputes.

scenes.name: Households on a hillside

convenience.note: The surveyor gets off the bus on River Road and knocks on the nearest doors.

voluntary.note: A flyer asks households to text their water bill. The ones angry about big bills answer most.

scenes.stratWhy: Hillside lawns use much more water than riverside yards, so each side of town is a stratum of similar households.
scenes.clusterWhy: Each street sits on one side of town, so the households on a street are alike: a few streets can land all on one side.
scenes.convWhy: River Road is on the riverside, where yards are small, so the nearest doors use less water than the town as a whole.
scenes.volWhy: The households with the biggest bills are the most eager to answer, so the responses run high.

scenes.name: Plots in a tomato field

convenience.note: The agronomist parks on the farm road along the west edge and measures the first plots she reaches.

scenes.noVoluntary: Plots of land cannot volunteer, so there is no voluntary response sample here.
scenes.stratWhy: The irrigated east grows far more than the dry west, so each zone is a stratum of similar plots.
scenes.clusterWhy: Every row crosses both zones, so each row looks like a small copy of the field: here a cluster sample works well.
scenes.convWhy: The farm road runs along the dry west edge, where plots are dusty and get no water from the canal, so they yield less.

scenes.name: Students in classrooms

convenience.note: The reporter surveys the class next to the main office, Room 101.

voluntary.note: An online poll asks, "Are you getting enough sleep?" The most tired students answer most.

scenes.stratWhy: Older students sleep less, so each grade is a stratum of similar students.
scenes.clusterWhy: Each classroom holds one grade, so a classroom is a group of similar students: one or two rooms can miss whole grades.
scenes.convWhy: Room 101 is a ninth grade class, and ninth graders sleep the most, so the sample runs high.
scenes.volWhy: The students who sleep least are the most eager to answer, so the responses run low.

contexts.lead: The student newspaper asks whether students want school to start later.
contexts.param: the proportion of all students who want a later start

strata.why: students in different grades may answer differently

contexts.conv: The editor stands at the cafeteria door at lunch.
contexts.convWhy: Students who eat in the cafeteria at that lunch period may feel differently from the rest of the school.
contexts.vol: The editor posts a link to an online poll, and 60 students choose to answer it.
contexts.volWhy: Students with strong feelings about the start time are the ones who bother to answer.

biases.text: The poll link is shared only by the club campaigning for a later start, and 300 students choose to answer it.
biases.why: Here the campaign reached its own supporters first.
biases.how: The students eager to answer are mostly the ones who want the change, so the sample proportion is likely higher than the true proportion.

biases.text: The editor picks 100 students at random from the list of students who ride the early bus.
biases.why: Students who do not ride the early bus can never be chosen.
biases.how: Early bus riders wake up earliest, so they are more likely than other students to want a later start.

biases.text: A random sample of 100 students gets the survey by email at 6 a.m., and the survey closes at 7 a.m. Only 38 answer.
biases.why: The 62 who did not answer were chosen but are missing.
biases.how: The students awake and answering before 7 a.m. are early risers, who are less likely to want a later start.

biases.text: Each of 100 randomly chosen students is asked, "Should the school stop forcing students through exhausting 7:30 a.m. classes?"
biases.why: The wording pushes students toward one answer.
biases.how: The loaded wording makes saying yes to a later start feel like the only reasonable answer.

contexts.lead: A town council wants to know how residents feel about a new bike lane.
contexts.param: the proportion of all households in the town that support the bike lane

strata.why: households in different neighborhoods may answer differently

contexts.conv: A council member walks down her own street, next to the downtown bike shop.
contexts.convWhy: Households next to a downtown bike shop may ride more, and like bike lanes more, than the rest of the town.
contexts.vol: The council asks residents in the newspaper to call in their opinion, and 80 households call.
contexts.volWhy: Households with strong opinions are the ones who call; most households never do.

biases.text: Volunteers with clipboards stand outside the downtown bike shop on Saturday and ask the people walking by.
biases.why: The people walking past a bike shop were the easiest to reach.
biases.how: People at a bike shop are more likely than the average resident to ride, so they support bike lanes more.

biases.text: The bike club's website invites visitors to vote on the bike lane, and 500 people vote.
biases.why: The voters chose themselves, and the site's visitors are mostly riders.
biases.how: Bike club readers favor bike lanes far more than the town as a whole.

biases.text: The council chooses households at random from the phone book, which lists only landline numbers.
biases.why: Households without a landline cannot be chosen.
biases.how: Landline households tend to be older and to drive more, so they are less likely to support a bike lane.

biases.text: Interviewers in bike club shirts ask a random sample of households, "You do want safer streets for our children, don't you?"
biases.why: The shirts and the leading question push the answer.
biases.how: Few people say no to "safer streets for children", so support looks higher than it is.

contexts.lead: An agronomist estimates this season's tomato harvest on a large farm.
contexts.param: the mean yield per plot on the farm

strata.why: sandy and clay soils grow tomatoes differently

contexts.conv: The agronomist parks on the farm road and walks to the nearest plots.
contexts.convWhy: Plots along the road get dust and foot traffic, so their yields may be lower than plots deeper in the field.

biases.text: The agronomist chooses plots at random, but only from the plots beside the irrigation canal.
biases.why: Plots away from the canal can never be chosen.
biases.how: Plots beside the canal get the most water, so they grow more than the average plot.

biases.text: The agronomist measures the 40 plots closest to the dusty farm road.
biases.why: Those were simply the easiest plots to reach.
biases.how: Roadside plots lose yield to dust and trampling, so they grow less than the average plot.

biases.text: Plots are chosen at random, but the farmer reports each plot's yield from memory and likes to round up.
biases.why: The values recorded are pushed in one direction.
biases.how: Rounding up every report makes the recorded yields higher than the true yields.

contexts.lead: A battery factory checks today's production for defects.
contexts.param: the proportion of all batteries made today that are defective

strata.why: the two machines may make defects at different rates

contexts.conv: The inspector reaches into the bin beside her desk.
contexts.convWhy: The batteries in the nearest bin all came from one short stretch of the day, so they may not match the rest.

biases.text: The inspector picks batteries at random from Machine A's log only, because Machine B's log is kept on paper.
biases.why: Batteries from Machine B can never be chosen.
biases.how: Machine B jams more and makes more defects, so leaving it out makes the defect rate look lower.

biases.text: The inspector tests the first 50 batteries off the line right after the morning cleaning.
biases.why: Those were the first and easiest batteries to grab.
biases.how: Freshly cleaned machines run best, so the first batteries are less likely to be defective.

contexts.lead: A hospital studies how satisfied patients were with their care.
contexts.list: the list of patients discharged last month
contexts.param: the proportion of all patients discharged last month who were satisfied with their care

strata.why: patients in different wards had very different stays

clusters.phrase: The 1500 patients left on 30 discharge days, 50 a day.

contexts.conv: The researcher waits at the follow-up clinic on Monday morning, where some of last month's patients come back for a check-up.
contexts.convWhy: Patients well enough, and near enough, to come back to the clinic on a Monday may have had different care from the rest.
contexts.vol: The hospital emails every patient a link to a feedback form, and 75 patients choose to fill it in.
contexts.volWhy: Patients with a very good or a very bad stay are the most likely to bother answering.

biases.text: A random sample of 150 patients is phoned. A third cannot be reached, most of them still recovering in a care home.
biases.why: The patients who were chosen but not reached are missing from the results.
biases.how: The patients still recovering likely had harder stays and lower satisfaction, so leaving them out pushes the estimate up.

biases.text: The nurse who treated each patient asks them, in person, whether their care was good.
biases.why: Patients answer to the person who cared for them.
biases.how: Few patients will tell their own nurse the care was poor, so satisfaction looks higher than it is.

biases.text: The hospital reads the forms left in the box by the exit marked "Comments and complaints".
biases.why: The patients who wrote forms chose themselves.
biases.how: A complaints box draws unhappy patients, so the forms show less satisfaction than patients really had.
